analysis.one_liner: Taxes every stock, bond, and derivative trade in the U.S., with rates rising to 0.1 percent.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2025 with 10 House sponsors, all Democrats, and was sent to the Ways and Means Committee, where it has had no hearings, votes, or further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would place a tax on each purchase of stocks, bonds, and derivatives traded on U.S. exchanges or by U.S. persons. The rate would start at 0.02 percent of the trade's value in 2026 and step up to 0.1 percent by 2030. Stock exchanges and brokers would be responsible for collecting and paying the tax, which exempts new stock and bond issues and very short-term debt. The revenue would go to the Treasury without being earmarked for any specific program.
analysis.who_benefits: The federal Treasury, which would gain a new revenue stream drawn from high-volume financial trading. To the extent the revenue funds public priorities, ordinary taxpayers benefit. Small, individual investors who trade rarely would pay only pennies on their occasional trades.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a tax on each covered purchase of stocks, partnership interests, bonds, and derivatives, starting at 0.02 percent of the trade's value in 2026 and rising in steps to 0.1 percent after 2029.

The tax reaches trades on U.S. exchanges and trades by U.S. persons even off-exchange, and treats foreign subsidiaries controlled by U.S. owners as U.S. persons, making it harder to shift taxable trades offshore.
Stock exchanges and brokers must collect and remit the tax for most trades, so individual investors would not have to calculate it themselves.
Exempts the initial issuance of securities, so companies raising new capital by selling stock or bonds do not pay the tax.

analysis.who_pays: High-frequency trading firms, hedge funds, banks, and other large investors who trade in enormous volume would bear most of the tax, since it applies to every covered transaction. Some of the cost would likely be passed through to ordinary investors through slightly higher trading costs in mutual funds and retirement accounts, and some trading might move to foreign exchanges to avoid it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wall Street trading firms and large investors

drawbacks.text: Because the tax applies to every covered transaction, including trades made by mutual funds on behalf of savers, a portion of the cost would flow to ordinary investors through higher trading costs inside 401(k)s and index funds.

Trading that can move to foreign exchanges or use instruments the bill exempts — such as debt with maturities of 100 days or less, which the bill excludes from the tax — could shift overseas or restructure to avoid it, shrinking the revenue and moving jobs and activity abroad.
The bill does not earmark its revenue for any specific purpose; the money would simply go into the general Treasury, so there is no guaranteed benefit tied to the new tax.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A 0.1 percent tax is small for a person saving for retirement but substantial for firms that trade billions of dollars daily, so the burden falls mainly on concentrated financial interests while the revenue could serve broad public purposes. The design is reasonably careful — it reaches offshore workarounds and exempts new capital raising — but its two real weaknesses are cost pass-through to small savers and the possibility that high-speed trading migrates outside U.S. exchanges.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee in June 2025 and has sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote ever since.

narrative.text: Rep. Val Hoyle and eight Democratic colleagues introduced the Wall Street Tax Act of 2025 in the House on June 17, 2025.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, which is where all tax legislation starts in the House.
Nine additional House Democrats signed on as cosponsors, bringing total support to 10 members of a 435-seat chamber.
The action history shows no further steps after the referral — no committee hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wall Street trading firms, exchanges, and large institutional investors are better off so far, because the bill has not advanced and no trading tax has been imposed. Ordinary people have neither gained nor lost yet, since the bill never reached a vote.

for.name: Rep. Val Hoyle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Wall Street Tax Act of 2025 and became its lead sponsor.

for.name: 9 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Jayapal, McGovern, Schakowsky, Tlaib, and Watson Coleman.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the bill has had no committee action since its referral in June 2025.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 sponsors and cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican or independent supports the bill, and Republicans hold 223 House seats and chair the committee that would act on it.

industries.industry: High-frequency trading firms and hedge funds
industries.note: The tax applies to every covered trade, so firms that trade billions of dollars daily would pay the most; high-volume traders could also simply relocate activity to foreign exchanges. Their gain from the bill stalling is the public's loss of potential revenue.

Exchanges are designated as the party that must collect and remit the tax on trades executed on their markets, and they would lose volume if trading migrates offshore. Their interest in keeping the bill off the floor runs against the Treasury's interest in the revenue.
Brokers must collect and pay the tax on off-exchange trades they execute for U.S. customers, adding compliance and trading-volume costs.
Fund managers' trading would be taxed, and some of that cost would pass through to savers in higher expenses, but the per-trade rate is small relative to fund returns.

analysis.trajectory: With only 10 House supporters, no Senate companion action, and Republicans controlling both the House majority and the Ways and Means Committee, this bill is very unlikely to receive a hearing or a vote this Congress. Unless it is attached to a larger tax bill or reintroduced with broader support, it will probably die when the session ends on January 3, 2027 — the usual fate of tax bills that never get a committee markup.
